beats.text: In November 1866, a new recruit signed up at an Army recruiting office in St. Louis, Missouri. Three years, in the regular Army.

overlays.hook: A Buffalo Soldier with a secret.

beats.text: The name on the papers was William Cathay. The medical exam was only a quick look.
William Cathay was a woman. Her real name was Cathay Williams.
For almost two years, she served in one of the Army's new Black regiments, the soldiers who became known as the Buffalo Soldiers.

visual.caption: Buffalo Soldiers of the 25th Infantry, Fort Keogh, Montana

beats.text: She is the only woman known to have served as one.
And when she was old and sick, and asked her country for a pension, it said no.
This is her story.
She was born in Independence, Missouri, in the 1840s. Her father was a free man. Her mother was enslaved, and so, under the law, was she.
As a girl, she worked as a house slave on a plantation outside Jefferson City, the state capital.
In 1861, the Civil War came to Missouri. Union troops occupied Jefferson City.
The Union army called the enslaved people it took in contraband of war. Many of them went to work for it, as cooks, laundresses and nurses.
Cathay Williams was about seventeen. She went to work for the Union army, cooking and washing for the soldiers.
She had to learn to cook on the job, first for officers.
She followed the troops for the rest of the war. In time she worked for the staff of General Philip Sheridan, one of the Union's best-known commanders.
She spent years around soldiers. She saw how they lived, how they marched, and how they were paid.
The war ended in 1865. She was free. She was also poor, and on her own.
After the war she went to St. Louis, and could not find steady work.
Years later, she told a newspaper why she did what she did next.
I wanted to make my own living, she said, and not be dependent on relations or friends.

visual.quote: I wanted to make my own living and not be dependent on relations or friends.

beats.text: In July 1866, Congress set the size of the peacetime Army. It created six regiments of Black soldiers. Two of cavalry, the ninth and tenth. And four of infantry, the thirty-eighth through the forty-first.
The new regiments would be sent west, to forts on the frontier.

visual.caption: A Buffalo Soldier of the 25th Infantry, Montana, 1880s

beats.text: Women could not enlist. So on November 15, 1866, in St. Louis, she enlisted as a man, William Cathay.
She signed up for three years, and was assigned to the thirty-eighth United States Infantry, Company A.

visual.caption: A Buffalo Soldier of the 25th Infantry, Company A, 1880s

beats.text: The recruiter wrote down her height, five feet nine inches, and her trade. Cook.
Only two people in the regiment knew her secret. In her words, a cousin and a particular friend.

visual.quote: Two persons, a cousin and a particular friend, members of the regiment, knew that I was a woman.

beats.text: Soon after she enlisted, she caught smallpox, and went into the hospital.
Her company went on without her, to Fort Riley, Kansas. She caught up with it later.
In the summer of 1867, Company A marched more than five hundred miles, from Kansas to Fort Union, in New Mexico Territory.

visual.caption: Santa Fe Trail ruts near Fort Union, New Mexico, today

beats.text: Fort Union guarded the Santa Fe Trail. Its walls still stand in ruins today.

visual.caption: Fort Union National Monument, New Mexico

beats.text: From there, the company marched hundreds of miles more, south, to Fort Cummings.
Fort Cummings sat in dry desert country in the southwest of the territory. Company A stayed about eight months.

visual.caption: The desert near Fort Cummings, New Mexico

beats.text: Across the West, the Buffalo Soldiers built roads, guarded posts and escorted the mail.

visual.caption: Buffalo Soldiers of the 25th Infantry, Fort Keogh, Montana

beats.text: Private Cathay was sick often. Army records place her in four different hospitals, on five separate occasions.
Each time, she was not found out.
Think about what that took. Every day, in a barracks full of men, on long marches and in sick wards, she kept her secret.
In June 1868, Company A marched to Fort Bayard, near Silver City, New Mexico.
Almost at once, she was in the post hospital again.
This time, the post surgeon discovered that Private William Cathay was a woman.
Almost two years of hiding were over.
On October 14, 1868, she was discharged at Fort Bayard, with a certificate of disability.
The paper never said she was a woman. It still called her he.
It said the soldier was of feeble habit, and often unfit for duty, and that the condition went back to before enlisting.
Her captain, Charles Clarke, signed it.

visual.caption: Signed by Capt. Charles E. Clarke, 38th Infantry

beats.text: She later said the men turned on her once they knew.

visual.quote: The men all wanted to get rid of me after they found out I was a woman.

beats.text: She had served in the Army for almost two years.
She did not go home. In 1869 and 1870, she worked back at Fort Union, as a cook for a colonel.

visual.caption: Fort Union National Monument, New Mexico, today

beats.text: Then she moved to Pueblo, Colorado, and married.
It did not last. Her husband stole her money and a team of horses. She had him arrested.
She settled in Trinidad, Colorado, and made a living as a laundress and a seamstress.
Years later, a reporter from St. Louis heard rumors about a woman who had served as a soldier, and came to interview her.
On January 2, 1876, the St. Louis Daily Times printed her story.
Why did she leave the Army? Her answer was plain. I got tired, and wanted to get off.

visual.quote: I got tired and wanted to get off.

beats.text: By 1890, her health was failing. She went into the hospital and stayed a long time, by one account nearly a year and a half. She came out with no money.
In June 1891, she applied for an Army pension, as a disabled veteran.
There was a precedent. Deborah Sampson had disguised herself as a man to fight in the Revolution, and the government had given her a pension.

visual.title: Deborah Sampson
visual.sub: a pension for a woman soldier

beats.text: A Pension Bureau doctor came to examine her. He found that her toes had been amputated. She could walk only with a crutch.
He ruled that she was not eligible. Her claim was rejected.
After that, she disappears from the record. No one knows when she died, or where she is buried.
For more than a century, her story sat mostly in Army files and pension papers at the National Archives.
In 1869, her old regiment, the thirty-eighth, was merged into the twenty-fifth Infantry, one of the Buffalo Soldier regiments that served on the frontier for decades.
In 2016, a bronze bust of her was unveiled in Leavenworth, Kansas, beside a rose garden.
The National Infantry Museum in Columbus, Georgia, added a bench in her honor on its Walk of Honor.
And today the National Park Service calls her the only known woman Buffalo Soldier.
She was born enslaved. She cooked and washed for one army through a war.
Then she joined another, under a man's name, because she wanted to make her own living.
She marched across the West, through sickness, and kept going.
And when it was over, she did not hide it. She told her story to a newspaper, in her own words.

visual.quote: I wanted to make my own living.

beats.text: On Veterans Day, remember her. Private Cathay Williams, thirty-eighth United States Infantry.
That was Cathay Williams. Subscribe for more.
